metaTitle: Thin Content: What It Is and How to Fix It
metaDescription: Thin content is a page that adds nothing a reader couldn't get elsewhere. Word count isn't the test. Here's the real test, and how to fix pages at scale.
definition: Thin content is any page that offers little or no value beyond what a reader could already get from the results around it, regardless of how many words are on it.
answer: Thin content is a page that adds nothing a searcher couldn't get elsewhere. Word count isn't the test — a 200-word answer can be excellent and a 2,000-word city page can be worthless. Google's spam policies target it directly under scaled content abuse and doorway pages, both of which are site-wide risks, not page-level ones.
takeaways: The test: **if this page vanished, would the searcher lose anything?** If not, it's thin at any length.
Google's scaled content abuse policy is method-agnostic — it's about the output, not the tooling.
Two hundred city pages where only the city name changes is exactly what that policy describes.
The fix is usually consolidation. Ten useful pages beat two hundred permutations.

sections.h2: Word count is the wrong measure
body: The "minimum 1,500 words" rule is folklore. It survives because it's easy to check and easy to bill for. A page answering "what is a 301 redirect" in 180 words, correctly, is a good page. Padding it to 1,500 makes it worse and slower.

The real question is comparative: **against the pages currently ranking for this query, does mine give the searcher something they'd otherwise miss?** Original data, first-hand experience, real prices, a clearer explanation, a decision they can act on. If the honest answer is "nothing, it's a rearrangement of the top three results", the page is thin, and length won't change that.

It's also why AI-drafted content isn't automatically thin and human writing isn't automatically fine. A human on their fortieth paraphrase of a competitor's blog post is producing thin content by hand.

sections.h2: Scaled content abuse, in Google's own words
body: In March 2024 Google rewrote its spam policies, replacing "spammy automatically-generated content" with **scaled content abuse**. The old wording could be argued around by saying a human touched the page. The new one targets generating many pages primarily to manipulate rankings rather than to help people — by automation, by humans, or by both.

That moved the line. Under the old wording an agency could produce 200 templated pages with a writer filling blanks and claim compliance. Now that's the exact behaviour described. Enforcement is rarely a dramatic manual penalty either — most sites see something quieter: pages dropping out of the index, crawl attention shrinking, good pages losing ground alongside the thin ones.

callout.title: It's a site-wide risk, not a page-wide one
callout.body: Thin pages don't just fail on their own — a large block of them changes what Google thinks your site is for. You can lose rankings on genuinely good pages because of pages you forgot you published.

sections.h2: The 200 city pages problem, which is also the doorway problem
body: Here's the version you'll actually be sold. Landing pages for every city you serve: "SEO services in Pune", "SEO services in Nashik", on to two hundred. One template, the city name swapped in six places, sometimes a landmark name-dropped. It's cheap to produce, the deliverable looks enormous on an invoice, and it occasionally works for a few months — which is why it keeps getting sold. Then a spam update lands and the whole folder goes.

Google's older doorway policy describes the same thing from another angle: a page built to catch a query variation and funnel the visitor elsewhere. The test is what happens after the click. If fifty location pages all say "we serve [city], contact us" and push to one form, the reader gained nothing by landing on the city version.

We run city pages ourselves, so let's be straight about the line. A city page earns its URL when it carries something true and specific that couldn't appear on any other city's page — the real competitive picture there, local search behaviour, pricing that reflects what businesses in that market actually pay. If we can't write that, we don't publish it. A [local SEO](/compare/local-seo-vs-national-seo) page that helps someone in Kochi decide is a destination; the same page with "Kochi" swapped for "Kollam" is a doorway.

Same test for service permutations: "affordable SEO services", "best SEO services" and "professional SEO services" as three URLs is one page and two [cannibalisation](/glossary/keyword-cannibalization) problems.

sections.h2: Fixing it: consolidate, improve, or cut
body: The remedy is the same however the thin pages got there. Inventory every URL, decide one of three things about each, and act in a single release.
numbered: **Consolidate.** Merge near-duplicates into one strong page and 301 the rest to it. Four thin service variants become one page that ranks for all four.
**Improve.** Keep pages where you can genuinely add something — real prices, real local detail, real experience. Rewrite them properly or don't keep them.
**Cut.** Remove pages with no traffic, no links and no purpose. Return 410 for dead URLs; 301 only where a real successor exists.
**Change the commissioning rule.** Noindex is a holding move, not a fix. If nothing changes about how pages get approved, you'll rebuild the same folder within a year.

callout.title: The one-line test to hand your agency
callout.body: Point at any page in the proposal and ask: what's on this that couldn't be on the other 199? If the answer takes more than five seconds, you're buying scaled content abuse.

faqs.q: How many words does a page need to avoid being thin?
faqs.a: There's no number, and any agency that quotes one is measuring the wrong thing. A 180-word definition that answers the query completely is fine. A 2,000-word page that restates the top three results is thin. The test is what the page adds, not how long it takes to say it.

faqs.q: Is AI-written content automatically thin content?
faqs.a: No. Google's stated position is that it judges content by quality and usefulness, not by how it was produced. AI-generated pages produced at volume to fill a keyword list are scaled content abuse. A well-researched piece drafted with AI assistance and carrying real information isn't.

faqs.q: Is there an actual thin content penalty?
faqs.a: There are two paths. A manual action for thin content or doorway pages appears in Search Console and requires a reconsideration request. More common is algorithmic suppression, which never announces itself — pages fall out of the index, crawl frequency drops, and nothing appears in your dashboard.

faqs.q: Are city or location landing pages always thin?
faqs.a: Only when they're identical. A location page carrying real market detail, local pricing and genuine reasons a business there would care is a legitimate page. A template with the city name swapped in is the textbook example of what the policy targets. The difference is entirely in the content.

faqs.q: Should I delete thin pages or improve them?
faqs.a: Improve the ones tied to something commercially real and consolidate the rest. Deleting is right when a page has no traffic, no links and no purpose. If you're deciding between merging and deleting, merging is safer — it preserves whatever link equity the URL collected.

faqs.q: How long does recovery take after removing thin content?
faqs.a: For an algorithmic suppression, weeks to months — Google has to recrawl the changed pages and reassess the site, and the reassessment often waits on a core update. A manual action can lift faster once a reconsideration request is accepted, but only if the cleanup is genuinely complete.
